{{short description|Unproven computational hardness assumption}}
In [[computational complexity theory]], the '''exponential time hypothesis''' or '''ETH''' is an unproven [[computational hardness assumption]] that was formulated by {{harvtxt|Impagliazzo|Paturi|1999}}. It states that [[3-SAT|satisfiability of 3-CNF Boolean formulas]] (3-SAT) cannot be solved in [[subexponential time]], <math>2^{o(n)}</math>. More precisely, the usual form of the hypothesis asserts the existence of a number <math>s_3 > 0</math> such that all algorithms that correctly solve 3-SAT require time at least <math>2^{s_3 n}.</math> The exponential time hypothesis, if true, would imply that [[P versus NP problem|P ≠ NP]], but it is a stronger statement. Beyond NP-complete problems, it implies that many known algorithms (including those with lower than exponential time) have optimal or near-optimal time {{nowrap|complexity.{{r|lms}}}}

==Definition==
The {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} problem is a version of the [[Boolean satisfiability problem]] in which the input to the problem is a [[Boolean expression]] in [[conjunctive normal form]] (that is, an ''and'' of ''ors'' of variables and their negations) with at most <math>k</math> variables per clause. The goal is to determine whether this expression can be made to be true by some assignment of Boolean values to its variables. [[2-satisfiability|2-SAT]] has a [[linear time]] algorithm, but all known algorithms for larger <math>k</math> take [[exponential time]], with the base of the exponential function depending on <math>k</math>. For instance, the [[WalkSAT]] probabilistic algorithm can solve {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} in average time <math display=block>\left(2-\frac2k\right)^n n^{O(1)},</math> where <math>n</math> is the number of variables in the given {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} {{nowrap|instance.{{r|s99}}}} For each {{nowrap|integer <math>k\ge 3</math>,}} define <math>s_k</math> to be the smallest number such that {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} can be solved in {{nowrap|time <math>2^{s_k n+o(n)}</math>.}} This minimum might not exist, if a sequence of better and better algorithms have correspondingly smaller exponential growth in their time bounds; in that case, define <math>s_k</math> to be the [[infimum]] of the real numbers <math>\delta</math> for which {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} can be solved in {{nowrap|time <math>O(2^{\delta n})</math>.}} Because problems with larger <math>k</math> cannot be easier, these numbers are ordered as {{nowrap|<math>s_3\le s_4\le \cdots</math>,}} and because of WalkSAT they are at most <math display=block>s_k\le \log_2 \left(2-\frac2k\right)<1.</math> The '''exponential time hypothesis''' is the [[conjecture]] that they are all nonzero, or equivalently, that the smallest of them, {{nowrap|<math>s_3</math>,}} is {{nowrap|nonzero.{{r|ip99}}}}

Some sources define the exponential time hypothesis to be the slightly weaker statement that 3-SAT cannot be solved in {{nowrap|time <math>2^{o(n)}</math>.}} If there existed an algorithm to solve 3-SAT in {{nowrap|time <math>2^{o(n)}</math>,}} then <math>s_3</math> would equal zero.  However, it is consistent with current knowledge that there could be a sequence of 3-SAT algorithms, each with running time <math>O(2^{\delta_i n})</math> for a sequence of numbers <math>\delta_i</math> tending towards zero, but where the descriptions of these algorithms are so quickly growing that a single algorithm could not automatically select and run the most appropriate one. If this were to be the case, then <math>s_3</math> would equal zero even though there would be no single algorithm running in {{nowrap|time <math>2^{o(n)}</math>.{{r|fg}}}} A related variant of the exponential time hypothesis is the '''non-uniform exponential time hypothesis''', which posits that there is no family of algorithms (one for each length of the input, in the spirit of [[advice (complexity)|advice]]) that can solve 3-SAT in {{nowrap|time <math>2^{o(n)}</math>.{{r|cef}}}}

Because the numbers <math>s_3,s_4,\dots</math> form a [[monotonicity|monotonic sequence]] that is bounded above by one, they must converge to a limit <math display=block>s_\infty=\lim_{k\to\infty} s_k.</math> The '''strong exponential time hypothesis''' (SETH) is the conjecture {{nowrap|that <math>s_\infty=1</math>.{{r|cip}}}}

==Implications==
===Satisfiability===
It is not possible for <math>s_k</math> to equal <math>s_\infty</math> for any {{nowrap|finite <math>k</math>:}} as {{harvtxt|Impagliazzo|Paturi|Zane|2001}} showed, there exists a constant <math>\alpha</math> such {{nowrap|that <math>s_k\le s_\infty(1-\alpha/k)</math>.}} Therefore, if the exponential time hypothesis is true, there must be infinitely many values of <math>k</math> for which <math>s_k</math> differs {{nowrap|from <math>s_{k+1}</math>.{{r|ipz01}}}}

An important tool in this area is the sparsification lemma of {{harvtxt|Impagliazzo|Paturi|Zane|2001}}, which shows that, for {{nowrap|every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>,}} any {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-CNF}} formula can be replaced by <math>O(2^{\varepsilon n})</math> simpler {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-CNF}} formulas in which each variable appears only a constant number of times, and therefore in which the number of clauses is linear. The sparsification lemma is proven by repeatedly finding large sets of clauses that have a nonempty common intersection in a given formula, and replacing the formula by two simpler formulas, one of which has each of these clauses replaced by their common intersection and the other of which has the intersection removed from each clause. By applying the sparsification lemma and then using new variables to split the clauses, one may then obtain a set of <math>O(2^{\varepsilon n})</math> 3-CNF formulas, each with a linear number of variables, such that the original {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-CNF}} formula is satisfiable if and only if at least one of these 3-CNF formulas is satisfiable. Therefore, if 3-SAT could be solved in subexponential time, one could use this reduction to solve {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} in subexponential time as well. Equivalently, {{nowrap|if <math>s_k>0</math>}} for {{nowrap|any <math>k>0</math>,}} then <math>s_3>0</math> as well, and the exponential time hypothesis would be {{nowrap|true.{{r|w03|ipz01}}}}

The limiting value  <math>s_\infty</math> of the sequence of numbers <math>s_k</math> is at most equal {{nowrap|to <math>s_{\operatorname{CNF}}</math>,}} where <math>s_{\operatorname{CNF}}</math> is the infimum of the numbers <math>\delta</math> such that satisfiability of conjunctive normal form formulas without clause length limits can be solved in {{nowrap|time <math>O(2^{\delta n})</math>.}} Therefore, if the strong exponential time hypothesis is true, then there would be no algorithm for general CNF satisfiability that is significantly faster than a [[brute-force search]] over all possible [[truth assignment]]s. However, if the strong exponential time hypothesis fails, it would still be possible for <math>s_{\operatorname{CNF}}</math> to equal {{nowrap|one.{{r|pw10}}}}

===Other search problems===
The exponential time hypothesis implies that many other problems in the complexity class [[SNP (complexity)|SNP]] do not have algorithms whose running time is faster than <math>c^n</math> for some {{nowrap|constant <math>c</math>.}} These problems include [[Graph coloring|graph {{mvar|k}}-colorability]], finding [[Hamiltonian cycle]]s, [[maximum clique]]s, [[maximum independent set]]s, and [[vertex cover]] on {{nowrap|<math>n</math>-vertex}} graphs. Conversely, if any of these problems has a subexponential algorithm, then the exponential time hypothesis could be shown to be {{nowrap|false.{{r|w03|ipz01}}}}

If cliques or independent sets of logarithmic size could be found in polynomial time, the exponential time hypothesis would be false. Therefore, even though finding cliques or independent sets of such small size is unlikely to be NP-complete, the exponential time hypothesis implies that these problems are {{nowrap|non-polynomial.{{r|w03|fk}}}} More generally, the exponential time hypothesis implies that it is not possible to find cliques or independent sets of size <math>k</math> in {{nowrap|time <math>n^{o(k)}</math>.{{r|chkx}}}} The exponential time hypothesis also implies that it is not possible to solve the [[3SUM|{{mvar|k}}-SUM]] problem (given <math>n</math> real numbers, find <math>k</math> of them that add to zero) in {{nowrap|time <math>n^{o(k)}</math>.}}
The strong exponential time hypothesis implies that it is not possible to find {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-vertex}} dominating sets more quickly than in {{nowrap|time <math>n^{k-o(1)}</math>.{{r|pw10}}}}

The exponential time hypothesis implies also that the weighted [[feedback arc set]] problem on [[tournament (graph theory)|tournaments]] does not have a parametrized algorithm with running {{nowrap|time <math display=inline>O(2^{o(\sqrt{\operatorname{OPT}})}n^{O(1)})</math>.}} It does however have a parameterized algorithm with running {{nowrap|time <math display=inline>O(2^{O(\sqrt{\operatorname{OPT}})}n^{O(1)})</math>.{{r|ks}}}}

The strong exponential time hypothesis leads to tight bounds on the [[parameterized complexity]] of several graph problems on graphs of bounded [[treewidth]]. In particular, if the strong exponential time hypothesis is true, then the optimal time bound for finding independent sets on graphs of {{nowrap|treewidth <math>w</math>}} {{nowrap|is <math display=inline>\bigl(2-o(1)\bigr)^w n^{O(1)}</math>,}} the optimal time for the [[dominating set]] problem {{nowrap|is <math display=inline>\bigl(3-o(1)\bigr)^w n^{O(1)}</math>,}} the optimum time for [[maximum cut]] {{nowrap|is <math display=inline>\bigl(2-o(1)\bigr)^w n^{O(1)}</math>,}} and the optimum time for {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-coloring}} {{nowrap|is <math display=inline>\bigl(k-o(1)\bigr)^w n^{O(1)}</math>.{{r|cfk}}}} Equivalently, any improvement on these running times would falsify the strong exponential time {{nowrap|hypothesis.{{r|lms}}}} The exponential time hypothesis also implies that any fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for [[Intersection number (graph theory)|edge clique cover]] must have [[double exponential function|double exponential]] dependence on the {{nowrap|parameter.{{r|cpp}}}}

===Communication complexity===
In the three-party set [[disjointness]] problem in [[communication complexity]], three subsets of the integers in some {{nowrap|range <math>[1,m]</math>}} are specified, and three communicating parties each know two of the three subsets. The goal is for the parties to transmit as few bits to each other on a shared communications channel in order for one of the parties to be able to determine whether the intersection of the three sets is empty or nonempty. A trivial {{nowrap|<math>m</math>-bit}} communications protocol would be for one of the three parties to transmit a [[bitvector]] describing the intersection of the two sets known to that party, after which either of the two remaining parties can determine the emptiness of the intersection. However, if there exists a protocol that solves the problem with {{nowrap|<math>o(m)</math> communication}} and {{nowrap|<math>2^{o(m)}</math> computation,}} it could be transformed into an algorithm for solving {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-SAT}} in {{nowrap|time <math>O(1.74^n)</math>}} for any fixed {{nowrap|constant <math>k</math>,}} violating the strong exponential time hypothesis. Therefore, the strong exponential time hypothesis implies either that the trivial protocol for three-party set disjointness is optimal, or that any better protocol requires an exponential amount of {{nowrap|computation.{{r|pw10}}}}

===Structural complexity===
If the exponential time hypothesis is true, then 3-SAT would not have a polynomial time algorithm, and therefore it would follow that [[P versus NP problem|P ≠ NP]]. More strongly, in this case, 3-SAT could not even have a [[quasi-polynomial time]] algorithm, so NP could not be a subset of QP. However, if the exponential time hypothesis fails, it would have no implication for the P versus NP problem. A [[padding argument]] proves the existence of NP-complete problems for which the best known running times have the form <math display=inline>O(2^{n^c})</math> {{nowrap|for <math>c<1</math>,}} and if the best possible running time for 3-SAT were of this form, then P would be unequal to NP (because 3-SAT is NP-complete and this time bound is not polynomial) but the exponential time hypothesis would be false.

In parameterized complexity theory, because the exponential time hypothesis implies that there does not exist a fixed-parameter-tractable algorithm for maximum clique, it also implies that {{nowrap|[[Parameterized complexity|W[1] ≠ FPT]].{{r|chkx}}}} It is an important [[open problem]] in this area whether this implication can be reversed: does {{nowrap|W[1] ≠ FPT}} imply the exponential time hypothesis? There is a hierarchy of parameterized complexity classes called the M-hierarchy that interleaves the W-hierarchy in the sense that, for {{nowrap|all <math>i</math>,}} {{nowrap|<math>\mathsf{M}[i]\subseteq\mathsf{W}[i]\subseteq\mathsf{M}[i+1]</math>;}} for instance, the problem of finding a [[vertex cover]] of size <math>k\log n</math> in an {{nowrap|<math>n</math>-vertex}} graph with {{nowrap|parameter <math>k</math>}} is complete {{nowrap|for M[1].}} The exponential time hypothesis is equivalent to the statement that {{nowrap|M[1] ≠ FPT}}, and the question of whether <math>\mathsf{M}[i]\subseteq\mathsf{W}[i]</math> for <math>i>1</math> is also {{nowrap|open.{{r|fg}}}}

It is also possible to prove implications in the other direction, from the failure of a variation of the strong exponential time hypothesis to separations of complexity classes.
As {{harvtxt|Williams|2010}} shows, if there exists an algorithm <math>A</math> that solves [[Boolean circuit]] satisfiability in time <math>2^n/f(n)</math> for some superpolynomially growing {{nowrap|function <math>f</math>,}} then [[NEXPTIME]] is not a subset of [[P/poly]]. Williams shows that, if algorithm <math>A</math> exists, and a family of circuits simulating NEXPTIME in P/poly also existed, then algorithm <math>A</math> could be composed with the circuits to simulate NEXPTIME problems nondeterministically in a smaller amount of time, violating the [[time hierarchy theorem]]. Therefore, the existence of algorithm <math>A</math> proves the nonexistence of the family of circuits and the separation of these two complexity {{nowrap|classes.{{r|w10}}}}

==See also==
*[[Savitch's theorem]], showing that a similar exponential gap cannot hold for [[space complexity]]
